Day 8: Ethereum attacks and the loot

questions.question_stem: A Monero payment's input is hidden in a ring of 16 outputs. An analyst wants to name the true spender from the ring and its key image. What do they give?
questions.correct_answer: Only that one of the 16 signed; the key image just stops a second spend of that output.
incorrect_answers: The oldest of the 16 is the true spender, because the decoys are all drawn from newer outputs.
The key image names the spender, so a second ring that reuses it gives the real input away.
The chain marks the true output in each ring, but the amount and the receiver stay hidden.
questions.explanation: The ring signature proves one member signed, not which; the key image only stops a double spend without revealing the output.

questions.question_stem: Two ransomware victims each paid a ransom, and in both payments an affiliate's share went to the same wallet. What does that suggest, and how firmly?
questions.correct_answer: One affiliate may have hit both victims; it is a lead that the shares suggest, not proof.
incorrect_answers: The developer attacked both victims itself, as the developer's share goes to one wallet.
Both victims paid the same ransom amount, which proves one group set a single price for them.
The developer kept 25% of each, so the shared wallet is proven to be the developer's.
questions.explanation: A shared affiliate wallet across two payments suggests one party hit both. The split shows on chain, but a shared wallet is a lead to check, not proof.

questions.question_stem: A hijacked cloud account mined coins, and the wallet earned about $8,000. The agent asks what the victim lost. What do you answer?
questions.correct_answer: The earnings are the attacker's take, not the loss; the loss is in the victim's cloud bills.
incorrect_answers: The loss equals the earnings, since whatever the attacker gained is exactly what the victim lost.
The loss is the wallet's earnings less the pool's fee, which the pool's statistics show.
The loss shows on chain as the payouts the pool made to the wallet over the period.
questions.explanation: Cloud cryptojacking turns a stolen account into a bill far larger than the coins earned. Report the earnings as earnings; the loss figure comes from the victim.

questions.question_stem: NFT #9 passed A to B to C to A three times, each move a paid sale, and one address funded all three wallets. How sure are you it is wash trading?
questions.correct_answer: Moderate: the paid sales are recorded and one funder stands behind both sides; a payoff would add more.
incorrect_answers: Low: a token cycling among a few wallets fits friends, own-wallet moves and buy-backs just as well.
High: three repeats of the same cycle prove it, and a later buyer or reward is not needed at all.
Not wash trading: sales at a recorded price between different wallets are real demand, nothing more.
questions.explanation: Paid sales with self-financed buyers put one party on both sides: Moderate. High needs the cycle repeated with a payoff, such as a later buyer, a ranking or reward tokens.

questions.question_stem: One transaction shows a large loan from a lending pool first, trades on two protocols, then a slightly larger repayment to that pool. No victim's loss is shown. What can you say?
questions.correct_answer: High that a flash loan was used; that it was an attack is open, as it may be arbitrage.
incorrect_answers: High that it was an attack, as a loan and repayment in one transaction show attacker intent.
Low that a flash loan was used, as the pool's own records are needed to confirm any loan.
Moderate for both claims, as a single transaction gives one kind of evidence for each.
questions.explanation: The transfers show a flash loan, so High for that. 'Attack' is High only with a victim's loss or the protocol's write-up; without either it may be arbitrage.

questions.question_stem: A call trace shows a pool's withdraw called again inside its own first withdraw, each paying the same contract, and the pool lost more than the caller put in. What does it show?
questions.correct_answer: Reentrancy: the pool paid again before it updated its record; Moderate from the trace alone.
incorrect_answers: A flash loan: the pool lent its whole balance out and was repaid inside the same transaction.
A price-oracle attack: the pool read a moved price and paid out against the wrong value.
Normal use: many legitimate contracts call back into a pool, so a trace shows nothing.
questions.explanation: The same function on the same contract called again inside its first call, each paying one contract, with a loss larger than the deposit, is reentrancy: Moderate from the trace, High with the write-up.

questions.question_stem: A lender reads its collateral price from one exchange pool. An attacker makes a huge trade on that pool, then borrows against the collateral. Why does the lender over-lend?
questions.correct_answer: It reads a price the trade moved; a time-weighted price or several sources would resist that.
incorrect_answers: It reads a stale price from an oracle network, so a faster price feed would have stopped it.
It trusts the borrower's own claim of value, so only a signed valuation would have stopped it.
It lets the borrower withdraw the collateral first, so only a repayment lock would stop it.
questions.explanation: DEX prices are open to manipulation, so a big enough trade moves the answer the lender sees, and a flash loan can pay for the trade. A time-weighted average price or several sources resists a recent large trade.

questions.question_stem: Decompiled code of an unverified contract says it can send every token to one address, and its logs show that it did. How sure are you of what it does?
questions.correct_answer: Moderate to High: the code says what can happen, and the logs agree that it really did.
incorrect_answers: Low: decompiled code is never evidence at all, unless the contract's source is verified first.
High from the code alone, since a decompiler gives back the original source exactly.
Moderate at most, whatever the logs show, as decompiled code alone is the ceiling.
questions.explanation: Decompiled code alone is Moderate at best; when the logs agree with it, the read rises to Moderate to High. Verified source with matching logs is High.

questions.question_stem: Funds left one ledger through a bridge and reappeared on another. What is the typology, and what is the hop in ATT&CK's terms?
questions.correct_answer: Chain-hopping; the hop is the technique, the how, and hiding the trail is the tactic, the why.
incorrect_answers: Chain-hopping; the hop is the tactic, the why, and the bridge it used is the technique.
A peel chain; the hop is the technique, the how, and the fresh change address is the tactic.
Layering by mixer; the hop is the procedure, one actor's way, and the tactic is the bridge.
questions.explanation: Chain-hopping is the typology: funds leave one ledger through a bridge or swap and reappear on another. In ATT&CK's shape the tactic is the goal (why) and the technique the means (how).

questions.question_stem: An analytics firm links a theft to North Korea. Two label sets agree, but both trace back to that firm's report. How many lines do you have, and how do you word it?
questions.correct_answer: One line; quote it as the firm's assessment, not a government attribution, at Moderate at most.
incorrect_answers: Three lines, so High; with all three agreeing it can be worded as the government's own attribution.
Two lines, so Moderate; the second label set comes from a separate firm and so counts on its own.
No lines, since labels from firms are never evidence unless a government confirms every one of them.
questions.explanation: Two sources that agree because one copied the other are one line: count origins, not labels. Quote the North Korea link as the firm's assessment.
